name: Inari Saami
sweep_summary: One title-hit for Inari Saami: Wiklund 1896, Entwurf einer urlappischen Lautlehre (MSFOu X). downloaded open copies from Fenno-Ugrica (handle 10024/89839, ABBYY text layer) and archive.org (suomalaisugrila04seurgoog); both with a manifest (also listing the 9/16 files already in the folder). The 'Accent' chapter (p. 123, page image checked) says word accent is on the first syllable in all present-day Saami dialects and therefore in Proto-Saami, with secondary-accent position undetermined; it is a pan-Saami/Proto-Saami statement with no Inari-specific accent data, so relevance is another language or variety and it merely confirms the catalog's fixed-dominant (initial) coding. Nothing left to acquire from this item (priority none). The catalog record's deciding citation is still empty (Wikipedia-sourced); the recommended deciding source remains Äimä 1918 §54.1 p. 80 ('Der hauptton oder gravis liegt bei isoliert ausgesprochenen Wörtern auf der 1. silbe'), read and filed in our reading of 9/16 ( / Aima1914 page images in the same folder), with Wiklund 1896:123 usable as family-level corroboration. all lookups were done with direct downloads (archive.org API, Fenno-Ugrica, HathiTrust API — the OCLC probe returned no HathiTrust record).

new_statements.quote: Der wortaccent liegt in allen jetzigen lappischen dialekten überall auf der ersten silbe des wortes. Wir können also schliessen, dass er auch in urlappischer zeit denselben platz gehabt hat, gewiss schon in der allerältesten urlappischen periode, da, wie bekannt, auch das finnische den wortaccent auf die erste silbe legt. In einem mehrsilbigen worte haben weiter ein oder vielleicht mehrere nebenaccente existieren müssen. Auf welcher silbe sie ihren platz gehabt haben, kann noch nicht ermittelt werden.
new_statements.translation: In all present-day Lappish [Saami] dialects the word accent lies everywhere on the first syllable of the word. We may therefore conclude that it had the same place in Proto-Lappish times too, certainly already in the very oldest Proto-Lappish period, since, as is well known, Finnish also places the word accent on the first syllable. In a polysyllabic word there must further have been one or perhaps several secondary accents. On which syllable they had their place cannot yet be determined.
new_statements.citation: Wiklund, Karl Bernhard. 1896. Entwurf einer urlappischen Lautlehre. I. MSFOu X. Helsingfors.
new_statements.locator: 'Accent', p. 123 (Fenno-Ugrica pdf page 135; page image verified)
new_statements.reading: Blanket family-level claim (1896) that every living Saami dialect, hence Inari Saami, has fixed initial word stress, with secondary-stress placement left open. It is consistent with the catalog's fixed-dominant/initial coding but is neither Inari-specific nor first-hand (Wiklund's own fieldwork was Lule Saami; his Inari data are second-hand). The only item in this search of works with stress in the title, so it is the best statement read today, but it should be cited only as corroboration.

new_statements.quote: 54. Das vorkommen der verschiedenen akzentstufen. — 1. Der hauptton oder gravis liegt bei isoliert ausgesprochenen wörtern auf der 1. silbe. [p. 81:] Wenn wir die sätze in sprechtakte einteilen, kann die 1. silbe eines jeden sprechtakts und nur diese in der regel als hauptbetont betrachtet werden. [...] 2. Der starke nebenton, gravior, scheint früher in der regel auf den ungeraden inlautssilben gelegen zu haben.
new_statements.translation: 54. The occurrence of the different accent grades. — 1. The main stress or gravis lies, in words pronounced in isolation, on the 1st syllable. [p. 81:] If we divide sentences into speech-feet, the 1st syllable of each speech-foot, and only this one, can as a rule be regarded as main-stressed. [...] 2. The strong secondary stress, gravior, seems formerly to have lain as a rule on the odd-numbered word-internal syllables.
new_statements.citation: Äimä, Frans. 1918. Phonetik und Lautlehre des Inarilappischen I-II. MSFOu 42-43. Helsinki: Suomalais-Ugrilainen Seura.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (initial stress = initial main stress) and as Wiklund 1896's pan-Saami statement; this is the first-hand, Inari-specific source and adds the secondary-stress rule (gravior on odd non-initial syllables, 3rd/5th), the five-grade system, the phrase-level (speech-foot) domain and the rhythmic exceptions, none of which the catalog records.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main (expiratory) stress is on the first syllable of every word pronounced in isolation; at phrase level the first syllable of each speech-foot (Sprechtakt) is the only main-stressed syllable, later words in the foot carrying only secondary grades. Äimä distinguishes five grades: 4 gravis (main), 3 gravior (strong secondary), 2 levior, 1 levis, 0 levissimus ('unstressed').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Strong secondary stress (gravior) on the odd-numbered non-initial syllables (3rd, 5th..), historically and still today wherever the original syllable count before that syllable is preserved (p. 82: 'Dieselbe akzentuationsregel hat auch für die jetzigen verhältnisse geltung, insoweit die ursprüngliche zahl der silben.. bewahrt ist'); in six-or-more-syllable words levior replaces gravior on the 3rd syllable for rhythmic reasons; the first syllable of the second member of a compound takes gravior (p. 81 n. 2); gravior on a final syllable implies apocope or contraction of the original final vowel (p. 82); where the rule seems not to hold, syncope or contraction earlier in the word is assumed (p. 83). §55 pp. 89-91 lists the attested word accent types by grade string, e.g. [40] pappi 'priest', [41] lodde 'bird', [42] monnim 'I went', [403], [4132] etc., all beginning with 4 on the first syllable. §63 p. 114: the musical (pitch) word accent of older speakers depends on the expiratory accent grades.
new_statements.exceptions: In lively speech a word that immediately follows a main-stressed monosyllable inside a speech-foot can take a stronger accent on its 2nd than on its 1st syllable (e.g. piso [41] in isolation vs. 1-2 in 'kauf mir eine gute flinte ab!'); Äimä attributes this to rhythm, not to lexical stress (p. 81). Anm. 2 p. 89: older speakers mark the secondary grades more energetically than younger ones. Anm. 1 p. 89: in double compounds levis replaces levior in some syllables for rhythmic reasons. Footnote 2 p. 80 cross-refers to Wiklund, Lärobok §17 f. and Nielsen, QuP 14 for the initial-stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Äimä describes Inari Saami proper ('unserem dialekt' = Inarilappisch), with examples tagged by sub-dialect/informant sigla (sS, sV, öM, öS, nAS, wHaM, wS etc; informants named on p. 114 include P. and I. Valle, M., A. and U. Sarre, Mannermaa, Aikio, Heikki Mattus, and S. Saijets). The main-stress rule is stated for the language as a whole; sub-dialect differences appear only in the secondary-grade details.

audit.recode_to: no reclassification of 'kind' (fixed-dominant, initial): confirmed by Äimä 1918 §54, Bye et al. 2009 p. 212, Türk et al. 2022 p. 891. Replace the Wikipedia citation with Äimä 1918:80 (§54.1) and Türk et al. 2022:891; if the catalog carries a secondary-stress/rhythm note, do not state 'binary feet, secondary stress on every odd syllable' -- per Äimä §54.2 and Bye et al. 2009 the secondary stress position is perturbed by historical syncope/apocope/contraction and is lexically/morphologically contrastive ((σ́σ) vs (σ́)(σ̀); tetrasyllables (σ́σ)(σ̀σ) or (σ́σσ)(σ̀)).

sources.citation: Wikipedia 'Inari Sami language', Phonology/Prosody section, re-read 2026-08-31
sources.quote: Inari Sami, like the other Samic languages, has fixed word-initial stress. Words are furthermore divided into feet, usually consisting of two syllables each, and with secondary stress on the first syllable of every foot.

sources.citation: Äimä, Frans. 1918. Phonetik und Lautlehre des Inarilappischen. I. Beobachtungsphonetik und deskriptive Lautlehre. Mémoires de la Société Finno-Ougrienne 42. Helsinki: SUS. (Fenno-Ugrica handle 10024/89873)

sources.quote: §54.1 (p. 80): 'Der hauptton oder gravis liegt bei isoliert ausgesprochenen Wörtern auf der 1. silbe.' p. 81: in a Sprechtakt only the 1st syllable is hauptbetont; in lively speech after a main-stressed monosyllable the 2nd syllable may exceptionally outrank the 1st ('durch rhythmische gründe bedingt'). §54.2 (p. 81-83): 'Der starke nebenton, gravior, scheint früher in der regel auf den ungeraden inlautssilben gelegen zu haben'; the rule still holds where original syllable count is preserved, but syncope, apocope and contraction yield present-day patterns with strong secondary stress on the 2n

sources.citation: Türk, Helen, Pärtel Lippus, Merit Niinemägi, Karl Pajusalu & Pire Teras. 2022. The durational structure of tetrasyllabic words in Inari Saami. Proc. Speech Prosody 2022, Lisbon, 891-895. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2022-181
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Words are mostly divided into feet following a trochaic pattern with a stressed initial syllable and a following unstressed syllable. Trisyllabic words in Inari Saami form a trisyllabic foot with two unstressed syllables following the primary stressed initial syllable.' Abstract: tetrasyllables 'are mainly divided into two disyllabic feet where the first two syllables form a primary stressed foot and the secondary stress is on the third syllable. However, a pattern where a trisyllabic foot is followed by a stressed fourth syllable also occurs' (contracted -eijee agent nouns).
sources.note: Most recent acoustic study; explicit English statement of trochaic initial stress and the two tetrasyllabic secondary-stress patterns; quotable replacement for the Wikipedia sentence.

sources.citation: Bye, Patrik, Elin Sagulin & Ida Toivonen. 2009. Phonetic duration, phonological quantity and prosodic structure in Inari Saami. Phonetica 66(4): 199-221. doi:10.1159/000298583 (author copy from carleton.ca/toivonen)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Main stress was still assigned to the first syllable, which in trisyllabic words formed a degenerate foot of its own ... Proto-Inari Saami *(σ́)(σ̀σ) > Inari Saami (σ́)(σ̀) ... The cumulative effect of metrical restructuring and apocope was thus the introduction of a new contrast that turned on the presence versus absence of a word-final monosyllabic foot: (σ́σ) vs. (σ́)(σ̀)' -- i.e. primary stress fixed initial; foot structure / secondary stress is lexically-morphologically specified, not purely alternating binary feet.
sources.note: Modern instrumental + metrical analysis stating main stress on the first syllable and showing secondary-stress/foot structure is contrastive ((σ́σ) vs (σ́)(σ̀)), which corrects the Wikipedia 'every foot two syllables' simplification.
